screens.title: Test-Driven Development (TDD) in Python
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn a disciplined way to design and verify Python code: Test-Driven Development, or TDD. TDD flips the usual workflow by asking you to write a focused test before you write production code. That failing test confirms the behavior you want, then you write the smallest code to satisfy it, and finally you refactor with the safety of your test suite. This process—Red, Green, Refactor—reduces guesswork, prevents over-engineering, and gives you rapid feedback as you develop. We'll use simple Python examples that mirror real practice: a Calculator add method and a StringUtil reverse method. You will see how tests guide design decisions, make refactoring safe, and serve as living documentation. We'll also cover practical tooling: using the built-in unittest or the more concise pytest, writing isolated unit tests, and avoiding common pitfalls like tests that depend on external state or implementation details. By the end of the chapter you will understand how to start each feature with a test, how to keep tests small and independent, and how to integrate TDD into your workflow so that refactoring becomes fast and low-risk. Consider how a failing test saves time by pointing directly at missing behavior—what would change in your next coding task if you began there?

screens.title: What is Test-Driven Development (TDD)?
screens.narratorSegment: Test-Driven Development is a development practice where tests are written before production code, and those tests drive the design and implementation of features. The test-first approach provides an executable specification: you state the expected behavior in code, run it to confirm it fails, implement the smallest change to satisfy the assertion, and then improve the code while keeping the assertions green. This changes the development rhythm: instead of guessing how code should behave, you start by expressing that behavior. A concrete example is a simple add function: first you write a test that asserts that adding two numbers equals their sum, run the test to see it fail, then implement the add method and run tests until they pass. A useful contrast is the traditional approach of writing code first and then tests: that often leads to regret when design assumptions are wrong. A common misconception is that TDD slows you down; on small tasks it may feel slower, but overall it saves time by preventing regressions and by making refactoring low-risk. For learners, start small, keep tests focused on behavior not implementation, and treat failing tests as a guide, not a punishment. How might your design change if every new feature began with an explicit failing test?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: TDD uses tests as the primary driver of design: tests first, minimal implementation, then refactor.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › What is TDD?
Definition
TDD is a cycle of writing a failing test, making it pass with minimal code, then refactoring while keeping tests green.
Why it matters
  • Tests act as executable requirements that reduce ambiguity.
  • Refactoring becomes safe because tests detect regressions immediately.
  • Design emerges from concrete examples rather than abstract planning.
Analogy
Think of each test as a unit test-case contract: it defines the behavior you expect and forces code to implement that contract.
Concrete example
# test_calculator.py
import pytest
from calculator import Calculator

def test_add_two_numbers():
    calc = Calculator()
    assert calc.add(2, 3) == 5
Run this test and watch it fail in the Red phase. The failure confirms the test expresses a missing behavior.
Key Takeaway

TDD forces clear expectations and gives a safety net for iterative design and refactoring.

screens.title: Red — Writing the failing test
screens.narratorSegment: The Red phase begins by writing a small, focused test that describes the new behavior you want and then running it to see it fail. This failure is essential because it confirms two things: the test actually asserts the behavior, and the behavior is not yet implemented. A useful concrete example is creating a test that imports a Calculator class and asserts that add(2, 3) returns 5. If the module or method doesn't exist, the test fails with a clear error such as a ModuleNotFoundError or AttributeError; that tells you you are correctly driving development. Common mistakes in this phase include writing a test that passes immediately or bundling many assertions into a single test. A passing test in Red means the test was not targeted at new functionality or it accidentally relied on an existing implementation. Good Red tests are tiny, fail for the right reason, and are easy to fix with minimal code. Treat the failing test as a specification: it tells you exactly what to implement next. Ask yourself: does my test fail for the expected reason, or is it masking a different issue?

keyIdea.title: Red phase
keyIdea.text: Write a failing, focused test that confirms the absence of the desired behavior—this failure directs your next minimal implementation.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Red Phase
Write a failing test
Create a minimal pytest or unittest case that asserts the behavior you want, then run the test to see it fail.
Common Red failures
  • ModuleNotFoundError when the module isn't created yet.
  • AttributeError when a class or method is missing.
  • AssertionError when the output doesn't match the expected value.
Common mistake
Writing tests that already pass or that couple to internal implementation prevents the Red phase from providing useful guidance.
Example test (Red)
# test_calculator.py
import pytest
from calculator import Calculator

def test_add_two_numbers():
    calc = Calculator()
    assert calc.add(2, 3) == 5
Run pytest now. Expect it to fail with ModuleNotFoundError or AttributeError. That failing output confirms your test is correctly targeted.
Key Takeaway

The Red phase validates your test as a specification; a useful Red test fails for the expected reason.

screens.title: Green — Implement the smallest change
screens.narratorSegment: In the Green phase you write the least amount of production code necessary to make the failing test pass. This often means a very small implementation, sometimes even a hard-coded return value for the specific test case. The purpose is to satisfy the assertion quickly so you can lock in behavior and move to refactoring. For example, after writing a test that expects add(2, 3) to equal 5, the simplest green implementation is a method that returns a + b. Resist the urge to generalize prematurely. Over-engineering in Green defeats the TDD purpose because it introduces complexity before tests demand it. After the test turns green, run the entire test suite to ensure no other tests fail. Green is not the finish; it is a checkpoint that confirms the behavior exists and that you can now safely improve the code. A misconception is that Green must produce production-ready code. Instead, Green is about minimal correctness. Once green, you refactor to improve structure, reduce duplication, and enhance readability with the confidence provided by passing tests. Green — Implement the smallest change means implement just enough code to make the failing test pass. prioritize minimal, verifiable change over perfection.. In practical terms, make the failing test pass with minimal code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Green phase
keyIdea.text: Implement just enough code to make the failing test pass. Prioritize minimal, verifiable change over perfection.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Green Phase
Make tests pass quickly
Write the simplest working implementation that satisfies the failing assertion. Minimal, verifiable changes are the goal.
Green guidelines
  • Implement the behavior described by the test and no more.
  • Run the full suite after making changes to detect regressions early.
  • Avoid premature generalization; refactor after green.
Pro tip
If a quick, simple implementation passes tests, accept it and plan required generalizations in refactor steps rather than in Green.
Example implementation (Green)
# calculator.py
class Calculator:
    def add(self, a, b):
        return a + b
Run pytest now. The specific failing test should pass. If other tests break, address them before refactoring further.
Key Takeaway

Green is about correctness against the test; it need not be the final design. Make it simple and verifiable.

screens.title: Refactor — Improve design with confidence
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring is the step where you improve the structure, readability, and performance of code after the tests are green. With a passing test suite you have a fast feedback loop: run tests after each small refactor to verify that behavior is unchanged. Effective refactoring goals include removing duplication, simplifying logic, improving naming, and extracting helper functions. A typical refactor sequence might convert a one-off implementation into a generalized method used by multiple tests, but you only introduce generalizations when tests indicate that expansion is needed. A common pitfall is to skip refactoring because tests are passing; that leads to fragile code over time. Another pitfall is refactoring too broadly without running tests frequently, which makes debugging harder. Always make small, verifiable changes and run the suite often. For example, once multiple add tests exist for positive, negative, and zero cases, you might refactor repeated setup into a fixture or extract validation logic, confirming after each change that all tests remain green. Refactor — Improve design with confidence means refactor to improve internal quality while the test suite prevents regressions; run tests frequently after each small change.. In practical terms, cleaning code while tests keep regressions at bay. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor phase
keyIdea.text: Refactor to improve internal quality while the test suite prevents regressions; run tests frequently after each small change.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Refactor
Refactor with the safety net
Once tests are green, improve code quality in small steps, running the suite after each change to catch regressions early.
Refactor checklist
  • Remove duplication and extract functions where meaning improves.
  • Rename variables and methods for clarity.
  • Introduce fixtures or helper utilities when tests repeat setup.
  • Run tests after each small change to localize failures quickly.
Misconception
Refactor is not optional. Passing tests are a reason to clean code, not to leave it as a temporary solution.
Example
After adding tests for negative numbers and zero, you may extract shared Calculator setup into a fixture and remove repeated code across tests.
Key Takeaway

Refactoring is safer with tests: iterate often, run the suite, and let tests guide structural improvements.

screens.title: unittest vs pytest
screens.narratorSegment: Python offers built-in unittest and the popular third-party pytest for writing tests. Both support test discovery, assertions, and fixtures, but they differ in ergonomics. unittest follows a class-based structure and requires subclassing TestCase for many patterns; it is stable and part of the standard library, making it available in any Python environment. Pytest tends to be preferred in TDD because it has a simpler function-based syntax, clearer failure output, and powerful fixtures that reduce boilerplate. For example, pytest allows a plain test function with asserts while unittest often requires assert methods and setup methods. In TDD the speed of writing a focused test matters, so pytest's concise style helps you iterate faster. That said, the TDD principles are the same regardless of framework: write a failing test first, make it pass, and refactor. Consider using pytest when you want quick, readable tests and rich plugin support; use unittest when you need strict standard-library compatibility. Remember: the choice of framework is secondary to maintaining small, isolated, behavior-focused tests. unittest vs pytest means pytest is concise and fixture-friendly; unittest is class-based and built-in. both support tdd if you keep tests focused on behavior.. In practical terms, choosing a python test framework for tdd. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › unittest vs pytest
unittest (built-in)
  • Part of the standard library; class-based tests and setup methods.
  • Predictable structure suitable for strict environments.
  • More boilerplate compared to pytest for common patterns.
pytest (recommended for TDD)
  • Function-based tests with plain assert statements.
  • Powerful fixtures for reusable setup and isolation.
  • Concise syntax speeds up test-driven iterations.
Example pytest snippet
import pytest
from calculator import Calculator

def test_add_two_numbers():
    calc = Calculator()
    assert calc.add(2, 3) == 5
Pytest's plain assert produces readable failure messages that help you diagnose why Red tests fail, which accelerates the TDD loop.

screens.title: Unit Test Isolation and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Test isolation means each unit test verifies a small piece of functionality independently of other tests and external state. Isolation makes tests fast and reliable; a flaky test that depends on file system state, network access, or global singletons undermines the TDD safety net. A practical strategy is to mock external dependencies, use temporary directories or fixtures for isolated resources, and avoid ordering dependencies between tests. For example, when testing a Calculator or StringUtil, ensure each test creates its own instance and does not rely on mutated shared data. Another best practice is to keep tests focused: one behavior per test and clear assertions. Tests should also prefer behavior-based assertions rather than checking internal implementation details; this makes refactoring easier. Speed matters in TDD: slow tests reduce the frequency you run the suite. Aim for fast, deterministic tests that give immediate feedback so you can iterate through Red-Green-Refactor quickly. Ask yourself: can this test run reliably in isolation on a CI worker without network access? Unit Test Isolation and Best Practices means keep tests independent, mock external dependencies, and focus each test on a single behavior to ensure speed and reliability.. In practical terms, make tests small, independent, and deterministic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Keep tests independent, mock external dependencies, and focus each test on a single behavior to ensure speed and reliability.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.6 › Test Isolation
Principles of isolation
  • Each test should be independent of others and produce the same result when run alone.
  • Mock or stub external systems like databases or network calls.
  • Use fixtures to manage setup and teardown deterministically.
Why it matters
Reliable, fast tests allow you to iterate frequently and trust the safety net during refactoring.
Example — isolate state
Create fresh objects inside each test and avoid shared mutable globals. If setup repeats, extract it into a fixture rather than relying on test order.
Key Takeaway

Isolated tests are fast, deterministic, and make debugging simple — essential qualities for effective TDD.

screens.title: Common TDD Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Experienced teams trip over a handful of recurring TDD pitfalls. The first is writing tests that are too broad—large integration-style tests that are slow and flaky, which discourage frequent runs. To avoid this, write narrow unit tests and add a few integration tests separately. The second pitfall is coupling tests to implementation details, which makes refactoring costly; instead assert observable behavior. Third, skipping the refactor step leaves working but messy code; treat refactoring as mandatory after Green. Fourth, writing too many tests before making any pass undermines the Red-Green rhythm—write one failing test at a time, make it pass, and repeat. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn a disciplined way to design and verify Python code: Test-Driven Development, or TDD. TDD flips the usual workflow by asking you to write a focused test before you write production code. That failing test confirms the behavior you want, then you write the smallest code to satisfy it, and finally you refactor with the safety of your test suite. This process—Red, Green, Refactor—reduces guesswork, prevents over-engineering, and gives you rapid feedback as you develop. We'll use simple Python examples that mirror real practice: a Calculator add method and a StringUtil reverse method. You will see how tests guide design decisions, make refactoring safe, and serve as living documentation. We'll also cover practical tooling: using the built-in unittest or the more concise pytest, writing isolated unit tests, and avoiding common pitfalls like tests that depend on external state or implementation details. By the end of the chapter you will understand how to start each feature with a test, how to keep tests small and independent, and how to integrate TDD into your workflow so that refactoring becomes fast and low-risk. Consider how a failing test saves time by pointing directly at missing behavior—what would change in your next coding task if you began there?

By the end of these lessons you will understand the fundamental principles of Test-Driven Development and be able to apply them in Python projects. First, you will learn the Red-Green-Refactor cycle as a disciplined loop for building features. Second, you will practice writing unit tests before production code and learn how tests can drive design decisions. Third, you will master how to write isolated, maintainable tests using pytest or unittest and how fixtures and small, focused tests make debugging and refactoring simple. Fourth, you will recognize common TDD pitfalls—tests that are too broad, tests tied to implementation instead of behavior, or skipping refactoring—and learn how to avoid them. Each objective includes an actionable milestone so you can measure progress: write a failing pytest test, implement minimal code to pass it, refactor safely, and add edge-case tests. These skills make code safer to change and provide living documentation for teammates. Consider a task where you must add a new feature: with TDD you start by expressing the expected behavior, run the test to confirm it fails, then implement and refactor with confidence.

You will demonstrate mastery by completing targeted practice tasks and by answering conceptual assessments. Practically, you will: write a failing pytest test for simple functionality, implement the smallest amount of code to pass that test, and then refactor with the tests running. You will expand tests to cover edge cases—empty strings, negative numbers, and palindromes for the StringUtil and Calculator examples. Good tests are narrow: they assert behavior, not internal state. Bad tests lock you to an implementation and make refactoring painful. As part of the milestone you will integrate your tests into a continuous integration setup so that every change runs the suite. The assessment will ask you to identify the Red phase goal, explain why Green should be minimal, and argue why refactoring must be guarded by tests. These outcomes ensure you can apply TDD reliably in team projects, reduce regressions, and maintain clean code over time.

Test-Driven Development is a development practice where tests are written before production code, and those tests drive the design and implementation of features. The test-first approach provides an executable specification: you state the expected behavior in code, run it to confirm it fails, implement the smallest change to satisfy the assertion, and then improve the code while keeping the assertions green. This changes the development rhythm: instead of guessing how code should behave, you start by expressing that behavior. A concrete example is a simple add function: first you write a test that asserts that adding two numbers equals their sum, run the test to see it fail, then implement the add method and run tests until they pass. A useful contrast is the traditional approach of writing code first and then tests: that often leads to regret when design assumptions are wrong. A common misconception is that TDD slows you down; on small tasks it may feel slower, but overall it saves time by preventing regressions and by making refactoring low-risk. For learners, start small, keep tests focused on behavior not implementation, and treat failing tests as a guide, not a punishment. How might your design change if every new feature began with an explicit failing test?

The Red phase begins by writing a small, focused test that describes the new behavior you want and then running it to see it fail. This failure is essential because it confirms two things: the test actually asserts the behavior, and the behavior is not yet implemented. A useful concrete example is creating a test that imports a Calculator class and asserts that add(2, 3) returns 5. If the module or method doesn't exist, the test fails with a clear error such as a ModuleNotFoundError or AttributeError; that tells you you are correctly driving development. Common mistakes in this phase include writing a test that passes immediately or bundling many assertions into a single test. A passing test in Red means the test was not targeted at new functionality or it accidentally relied on an existing implementation. Good Red tests are tiny, fail for the right reason, and are easy to fix with minimal code. Treat the failing test as a specification: it tells you exactly what to implement next. Ask yourself: does my test fail for the expected reason, or is it masking a different issue?

In the Green phase you write the least amount of production code necessary to make the failing test pass. This often means a very small implementation, sometimes even a hard-coded return value for the specific test case. The purpose is to satisfy the assertion quickly so you can lock in behavior and move to refactoring. For example, after writing a test that expects add(2, 3) to equal 5, the simplest green implementation is a method that returns a + b. Resist the urge to generalize prematurely. Over-engineering in Green defeats the TDD purpose because it introduces complexity before tests demand it. After the test turns green, run the entire test suite to ensure no other tests fail. Green is not the finish; it is a checkpoint that confirms the behavior exists and that you can now safely improve the code. A misconception is that Green must produce production-ready code. Instead, Green is about minimal correctness. Once green, you refactor to improve structure, reduce duplication, and enhance readability with the confidence provided by passing tests. Green — Implement the smallest change means implement just enough code to make the failing test pass. prioritize minimal, verifiable change over perfection.. In practical terms, make the failing test pass with minimal code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Refactoring is the step where you improve the structure, readability, and performance of code after the tests are green. With a passing test suite you have a fast feedback loop: run tests after each small refactor to verify that behavior is unchanged. Effective refactoring goals include removing duplication, simplifying logic, improving naming, and extracting helper functions. A typical refactor sequence might convert a one-off implementation into a generalized method used by multiple tests, but you only introduce generalizations when tests indicate that expansion is needed. A common pitfall is to skip refactoring because tests are passing; that leads to fragile code over time. Another pitfall is refactoring too broadly without running tests frequently, which makes debugging harder. Always make small, verifiable changes and run the suite often. For example, once multiple add tests exist for positive, negative, and zero cases, you might refactor repeated setup into a fixture or extract validation logic, confirming after each change that all tests remain green. In practical terms, cleaning code while tests keep regressions at bay. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Python offers built-in unittest and the popular third-party pytest for writing tests. Both support test discovery, assertions, and fixtures, but they differ in ergonomics. unittest follows a class-based structure and requires subclassing TestCase for many patterns; it is stable and part of the standard library, making it available in any Python environment. Pytest tends to be preferred in TDD because it has a simpler function-based syntax, clearer failure output, and powerful fixtures that reduce boilerplate. For example, pytest allows a plain test function with asserts while unittest often requires assert methods and setup methods. In TDD the speed of writing a focused test matters, so pytest's concise style helps you iterate faster. Test isolation means each unit test verifies a small piece of functionality independently of other tests and external state. Isolation makes tests fast and reliable; a flaky test that depends on file system state, network access, or global singletons undermines the TDD safety net. A practical strategy is to mock external dependencies, use temporary directories or fixtures for isolated resources, and avoid ordering dependencies between tests. For example, when testing a Calculator or StringUtil, ensure each test creates its own instance and does not rely on mutated shared data.
